newsitem.title: UK: Drugs new scourge for grieving Welsh village.
newsitem.headline: Drugs new scourge for grieving Welsh village.

text.p: On the day Aberfan remembered a generation of children wiped out by a coal tip disaster, villagers now battling the scourge of drugs buried a young man who hanged himself from a tree.
Thirty years ago, the world turned in pity to support this tight-knit Welsh mining community when a coal tip collapsed on the village school, killing 116 children and 28 adults.
On Monday, survivors and relatives returned to the hillside cemetery to commemorate those children who suffocated in a sea of black mud.

Just two hours later, mourners streamed up the hill for the poignant funeral service of a 23-year-old suicide victim in a village where the desperate and disillusioned young jobless have turned to drugs and crime.
But there was a ray of hope that linked these two very different tragedies, one played out in the full glare of international publicity, the other enacted in more private grief.
Jeff Edwards, the last of 10 children plucked to safety from the shattered wreckage of Aberfan school, is now running a drop- in centre for the jobless teenagers living without hope.
Edwards, a fiercely energetic councillor and magistrate, is determined to breathe life back into the village where the unemployment rate has soared to 25 percent.
"The kids don't know what to do. They have no work, no self- esteem. They turn to drugs as a release from their non-existent lifestyles. They feel themselves totally alienated from society," he said.
"The unemployment triggers the drugs and the crime to feed the habit. They have no self-esteem and are full of hopelessness and despair," he added.

Edwards, still trying to articulate his own grief 30 years after he lost his own childhood at the age of eight, was in reflective mood after the two sharply contrasting services in the village cemetery.
"We have had two deaths from drugs -- we had a heroin overdose and another under the influence of drugs crashed into a brick wall and killed himself when joyriding.
"Now we have this suicide. They must be in a desperate state to hang themselves in public as he did."

Edwards will not give in to despair. With more than 100,000 pounds ($160,000) of state and European Community funds, he renovated a dilapidated Presbyterian church in the village where the last coal mine closed in 1989 with the loss of 600 jobs.
Now the teenagers that once wandered the streets aimlessly can drop in for everything from literacy and computer classes to drug support groups or just a game of snooker.
"Back in 1966 there were jobs to go to and they had self- esteem. The only drugs we had 30 years ago were those you could find in the chemist shop," said Edwards.
"Today we have had children of 10 using cannabis. Heroin has come in during the last 12 months. I don't think the parents are facing reality."
Thirty years after his own life was spared, the 38-year-old magistrate is determined to build a future for the next generation even if it is a tough battle.
Looking around the drop-in centre, he ruefully admitted: "If all this fails, I'll see them in court and in prison as well as I'm on the board of governors."
